newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Europe, Japan to hold fast despite U.S. rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Europe, Japan to hold fast despite U.S. rise.

text.p: Europe and Japan are unlikely to follow the United States in raising interest rates in the near future, their economies still too fragile to warrant tighter monetary policies, analysts said on Wednesday.
The Federal Reserve's quarter point rate rise on Tuesday made clear the disparity between the vibrant U.S. economy and economies in most of Europe and Japan, still struggling to spring into action.

"It's very much an isolated event," John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International in London. "It really does reflect the fact that the U.S. economy is at a completely different stage in the economic cycle than the other global blocks."

The Federal Reserve raised it's federal funds rate to 5.50 percent on Tuesday, calling the move a "prudent step" to help prolong the economic expansion by sustaining the existing low inflationary environment.

Economies in Europe and Japan have low inflationary environments, too, but due to weak growth. in contrast the U.S. economy is in its sixth year of expansion and is expected to have grown around 3.0 percent in the first quarter.
Germany has benefited from a weaker mark and rising exports this year but analysts see growth of only around 2.2 percent.

Unemployment is still soaring across much of Europe and, more importantly for interest rates, inflation is minimal. Only in Britain are interest rates likely to rise this year -- after the May 1 national election, analysts said.
"The only comparison which does appply is that between the U.S. and U.K," Shepperd said.
The British economy is bubbling away at brisk pace. It posted growth of 2.6 percent in the fourth quarter of last year and an inflation rate of 2.7 percent in February.

Ian McCafferty, director of international economics at NatWest Capital Markets in London, said a 50 basis point rise to Britain's 6.0 percent base rate would be enough to ward off an upsurge in inflation -- if it was accompanied by fiscal cuts.

Japan, struggling with fiscal reform and set to raise its consumption tax on April 1, expects real growth of 1.9 percent this year. It's official discount rate is unlikely to budge from 0.50 percent soon, analysts said.

"It's clear from recent statements from the central bank of the need to keep liquidity levels high and hence short rates and the bond market rates as low as possible for some time in order to deal with continuing structural problelms," McCafferty said.
Even an upsurge in the dollar against European currencies or the yen on the back of a U.S. rate rise, was unlikely to spur central banks into action, analysts said.
Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London, expected verbal support for the mark and the yen first, then central bank intervention. A supportive rate rise was unlikely.
"It's very unusual for the Bundesbank to move interest rates for foreign exchange reasons...unless the economy does show signs of resurging," he said.
Sheppard at Yamaichi agreed, adding the dollar had moved little before the widely expected Fed move or after.
"If you look at the action in the currency markets it does tell us the dollar has already seen it's peak and 1.75 against the mark and 125 against the yen is unlikely to be exceeded," he said.
The dollar was quoted at 1.6925 marks at 1355 GMT, down from 1.6928/33 in late European trading on Tuesday and at 124.14 yen, after stalling overnight around 124.35.
